statement: Let $f$ be an [entire function](c:entire-function), not identically zero, with a zero of order $m \ge 0$ at $0$ and other zeros $a_1, a_2, \dots$ listed with multiplicity. Then $f(z) = z^m e^{g(z)} \prod_n E_{n-1}(z/a_n)$ for an entire $g$, where $E_p(u) = (1-u)\exp(u + u^2/2 + \dots + u^p/p)$, and the [infinite product](c:infinite-product) converges [locally uniformly](c:locally-uniform-convergence).

hypotheses.text: The function $f\colon \mathbb{C} \to \mathbb{C}$ is [entire](c:entire-function).
The function $f$ is not identically zero.

conclusion: Some entire function $g$ gives $f(z) = z^m e^{g(z)} \prod_n E_{n-1}(z/a_n)$, and the product converges locally uniformly on $\mathbb{C}$.

proofs.name: Elementary factors and a logarithm
proofs.slogan: Build an entire product with exactly the zeros of $f$ from elementary factors, then write the zero-free quotient as an exponential.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem. With finitely many zeros the product is finite, and with no zeros away from $0$ it is empty, so $f = z^m e^{g}$.

roles.why: Holomorphy gives isolated zeros of finite order and a holomorphic $h'/h$ for the zero-free quotient.
A function that is not identically zero has isolated zeros, so they form a sequence with $|a_n| \to \infty$.

steps.slogan: List the zeros of $f$ as a sequence whose moduli tend to infinity.
steps.detail: By the identity theorem the zeros of the nonzero [entire function](c:entire-function) $f$ are isolated and of finite order, so each disc holds finitely many. Listed with multiplicity they satisfy $0 < |a_1| \le |a_2| \le \dots$ and $|a_n| \to \infty$ when there are infinitely many.

steps.slogan: Bound each elementary factor by $|1 - E_p(u)| \le |u|^{p+1}$ for $|u| \le 1$.
steps.detail: The derivative is $E_p'(u) = -u^p \exp(u + \dots + u^p/p)$, so $1 - E_p(u) = u^{p+1}\psi(u)$ where $\psi$ has nonnegative Taylor coefficients. Then $|\psi(u)| \le \psi(1) = 1 - E_p(1) = 1$ for $|u| \le 1$.

steps.slogan: Show that the product $P(z) = \prod_n E_{n-1}(z/a_n)$ converges locally uniformly.
steps.detail: On $|z| \le R$ all but finitely many $n$ have $|a_n| \ge 2R$, so step 2 gives $|1 - E_{n-1}(z/a_n)| \le 2^{-n}$. A product $\prod(1 - u_n)$ with $\sum |u_n|$ uniformly convergent converges uniformly, so the [infinite product](c:infinite-product) $P$ is entire.

steps.slogan: Check that $z^m P(z)$ has exactly the zeros of $f$ with the same orders.
steps.detail: On each disc the tail of the product converges [locally uniformly](c:locally-uniform-convergence) to a function without zeros, and $E_{n-1}(z/a_n)$ vanishes only at $a_n$, simply. So $h = f/(z^m P)$ has removable singularities and extends to a zero-free entire function.

steps.slogan: Write the zero-free quotient $h$ as $e^{g}$ with $g$ entire.
steps.detail: The function $h'/h$ is entire and $\mathbb{C}$ is [simply connected](c:simply-connected-space), so $h'/h$ has an entire primitive $g_0$ by Cauchy's theorem. Then $(h e^{-g_0})' = 0$, so $h = e^{g}$ with $g = g_0 + c$, and $f = z^m e^{g} P$.

concepts.c:entire-function: The function and the product are entire, so their quotient is entire.
concepts.c:infinite-product: The infinite product supplies an entire function with prescribed zeros.
concepts.c:locally-uniform-convergence: Locally uniform convergence makes the product holomorphic and controls its zeros.
concepts.c:simply-connected-space: Simple connectivity of the plane gives a logarithm of the zero-free quotient.

source.note: The classical proof with Weierstrass elementary factors, as in W. Rudin, Real and Complex Analysis, chapter 15.

statement: Let $(M_i)_{i \in I}$ be nonempty $L$-[structures](c:structure-model-theory), $\mathcal{U}$ an [ultrafilter](c:ultrafilter) on $I$ and $M = \prod_i M_i/\mathcal{U}$ their [ultraproduct](c:ultraproduct). For every [first-order](c:first-order-logic) formula $\varphi(x_1, \dots, x_n)$ and $a^1, \dots, a^n \in \prod_i M_i$, $M \models \varphi([a^1], \dots, [a^n])$ if and only if $\{i : M_i \models \varphi(a^1_i, \dots, a^n_i)\} \in \mathcal{U}$.

hypotheses.text: Each $M_i$ is a nonempty [structure](c:structure-model-theory) for the signature $L$.
The family $\mathcal{U}$ is an [ultrafilter](c:ultrafilter) on the index set $I$.
The formula $\varphi$ is a [first-order](c:first-order-logic) formula of $L$.

conclusion: The formula $\varphi$ holds at $([a^1], \dots, [a^n])$ in $M$ exactly when it holds at $(a^1_i, \dots, a^n_i)$ in the factors $M_i$ for a set of indices $i$ in $\mathcal{U}$.

proofs.name: Induction on formulas
proofs.slogan: Prove the equivalence for atomic formulas from the definition of the ultraproduct, then carry it through negation, conjunction and the existential quantifier.
proofs.scope: All first-order formulas built with $\neg$, $\wedge$ and $\exists$, the other connectives and $\forall$ being abbreviations. The case $n = 0$ gives the statement for sentences.

roles.why: Nonempty factors make $\prod_i M_i$ nonempty and supply arbitrary values where no witness is needed.
The [filter](c:filter) axioms handle atomic formulas and conjunction, and maximality handles negation.
First-order formulas arise from atomic ones by finitely many rules, so induction on their construction reaches all of them.

steps.slogan: Check the equivalence for atomic formulas with the definition of the ultraproduct.
steps.detail: Elements of $M$ are classes for $a \sim b \iff \{i : a_i = b_i\} \in \mathcal{U}$, and symbols act coordinatewise; the [filter](c:filter) axioms make this well defined. Induction on terms gives $t^M([a]) = [(t^{M_i}(a_i))_i]$, so $t_1 = t_2$ and $R(t_1, \dots, t_k)$ hold in $M$ exactly when they hold on a set in $\mathcal{U}$.

steps.slogan: Pass the equivalence through negation with the maximality of the ultrafilter.
steps.detail: Let $A$ be the set of $i$ where $\varphi$ holds in $M_i$. Exactly one of $A$ and $I \setminus A$ lies in the [ultrafilter](c:ultrafilter) $\mathcal{U}$, so $M \models \neg\varphi$ iff $A \notin \mathcal{U}$ iff $I \setminus A \in \mathcal{U}$.

steps.slogan: Pass the equivalence through conjunction with closure under intersections and supersets.
steps.detail: A filter contains $A \cap B$ iff it contains both $A$ and $B$, because it is closed under finite intersections and supersets. Applied to the truth sets of $\varphi$ and $\psi$, this gives the case $\varphi \wedge \psi$.

steps.slogan: Choose witnesses coordinatewise to pass the equivalence through the existential quantifier.
steps.detail: If $M \models \varphi([b], [a])$, then $\varphi(b_i, a_i)$ holds on a set in $\mathcal{U}$, inside the truth set of $\exists y\,\varphi$. Conversely, if $\exists y\,\varphi(y, a_i)$ holds on $A \in \mathcal{U}$, the [axiom of choice](c:axiom-of-choice) picks witnesses $b_i$ for $i \in A$ and arbitrary $b_i$ elsewhere, and $[b]$ is a witness in $M$.

steps.slogan: Combine the four cases by induction on the construction of the formula.
steps.detail: Every [first-order](c:first-order-logic) formula is atomic or comes from shorter formulas by $\neg$, $\wedge$ or $\exists$. Steps 1 to 4 prove the equivalence for each construction from the equivalence for its parts, for all tuples at once, so it holds for every formula.

concepts.c:structure-model-theory: The factors and the ultraproduct are structures in which formulas are evaluated.
concepts.c:ultrafilter: Ultrafilter maximality makes truth sets decide negation.
concepts.c:ultraproduct: The ultraproduct is the structure whose truth the theorem computes.
concepts.c:first-order-logic: The induction runs over the rules that build first-order formulas.
concepts.c:filter: Closure under intersections and supersets gives well-definedness and conjunction.
concepts.c:axiom-of-choice: Choice selects a witness in each factor for the existential step.

source.note: The standard induction on formulas, as in C. C. Chang and H. J. Keisler, Model Theory, section 4.1.

statement: Let $f_0, f_1, \dots$ and $g_0, g_1, \dots$ be real or complex numbers with [partial sums](c:partial-sum) $G_k = \sum_{i<k} g_i$, and let $m < n$. Then $\sum_{i=m}^{n-1} f_i g_i = f_{n-1} G_n - f_m G_m - \sum_{i=m}^{n-2} (f_{i+1} - f_i)\, G_{i+1}$.

hypotheses.text: The terms $f_i$ and $g_i$ are real or complex numbers.
The summation bounds satisfy $m < n$.

conclusion: The [finite sum](c:finite-sum) $\sum_{i=m}^{n-1} f_i g_i$ equals $f_{n-1} G_n - f_m G_m - \sum_{i=m}^{n-2} (f_{i+1} - f_i) G_{i+1}$.

formal.difference: The declaration allows the f_i in any ring and the g_i in any module over it; the statement here takes real or complex numbers.

proofs.name: Differences of partial sums
proofs.slogan: Write each $g_i$ as a difference of partial sums, split the sum in two and shift the index of one part.
proofs.scope: The whole identity. For $n = m + 1$ the last sum is empty and the identity reads $f_m g_m = f_m (G_{m+1} - G_m)$.

roles.why: Numbers obey the distributive and associative laws that every regrouping uses.
The bound $m < n$ gives $m \le n - 1$, so the boundary terms $f_{n-1} G_n$ and $f_m G_m$ split off.

steps.slogan: Write each term $g_i$ as the difference $G_{i+1} - G_i$ of partial sums.
steps.detail: By definition $G_0 = 0$ and $G_{i+1} = G_i + g_i$, so $g_i = G_{i+1} - G_i$ for every $i \ge 0$. Hence $f_i g_i = f_i G_{i+1} - f_i G_i$.

steps.slogan: Split the sum into $\sum f_i G_{i+1}$ minus $\sum f_i G_i$ over $m \le i \le n - 1$.
steps.detail: Summing step 1 over $m \le i \le n - 1$ gives $\sum_{i=m}^{n-1} f_i g_i = \sum_{i=m}^{n-1} f_i G_{i+1} - \sum_{i=m}^{n-1} f_i G_i$, a difference of two [finite sums](c:finite-sum).

steps.slogan: Shift the index of the second sum and split off the boundary terms.
steps.detail: Because $m \le n - 1$, the first sum is $\sum_{i=m}^{n-2} f_i G_{i+1} + f_{n-1} G_n$. The substitution $i \mapsto i + 1$ turns the second sum into $f_m G_m + \sum_{i=m}^{n-2} f_{i+1} G_{i+1}$.

steps.slogan: Subtract the two sums and collect the coefficient of each $G_{i+1}$.
steps.detail: The difference is $f_{n-1} G_n - f_m G_m + \sum_{i=m}^{n-2} (f_i - f_{i+1}) G_{i+1}$, which is the stated right side.

concepts.c:partial-sum: Partial sums replace the terms through $g_i = G_{i+1} - G_i$.
concepts.c:finite-sum: The identity regroups finite sums, so every rearrangement is exact.

statement: Let $K$ be a [field](c:field) of characteristic $0$ and $n \ge 5$. The general polynomial $x^n - t_1 x^{n-1} + \dots + (-1)^n t_n$ over $K(t_1, \dots, t_n)$, with independent indeterminates $t_i$ as coefficients, is not solvable by radicals: none of its roots lies in a radical extension of $K(t_1, \dots, t_n)$.

hypotheses.text: The [field](c:field) $K$ has characteristic $0$.
The degree satisfies $n \ge 5$.
The coefficients $t_1, \dots, t_n$ are independent indeterminates over $K$.

conclusion: No root of the general polynomial of degree $n$ lies in a radical extension of $K(t_1, \dots, t_n)$.

formal.difference: The declaration proves one direction only: an irreducible polynomial with a root in a radical extension has a solvable Galois group. It does not compute the Galois group of the general polynomial or show that S_n is not solvable.

proofs.name: Galois group of the general polynomial
proofs.slogan: The general polynomial has Galois group $S_n$, a root by radicals forces a solvable Galois group, and $S_n$ is not solvable for $n \ge 5$.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem. The degree bound enters only in step 3; for $n \le 4$ the group $S_n$ is solvable and formulas by radicals exist.

roles.why: Characteristic $0$ makes every extension separable, so each radical step with enough roots of unity is Galois with abelian group.
For $n \ge 5$ there are five distinct letters, which every $3$-cycle commutator needs.
Independent coefficients make every permutation of the roots a field automorphism.

steps.slogan: Compute the [Galois group](c:galois-group) of the general polynomial as the [symmetric group](c:symmetric-group) $S_n$.
steps.detail: Let $x_1, \dots, x_n$ be indeterminates with [elementary symmetric polynomials](c:elementary-symmetric-polynomial) $s_k$. These are algebraically independent, so $t_k \mapsto s_k$ identifies $K(t)$ with $K(s)$ and the general polynomial with $\prod_i (x - x_i)$, whose splitting field is $K(x_1, \dots, x_n)$. Every permutation of the $x_i$ fixes $K(s)$, so the group is $S_n$.

steps.slogan: Show that a root in a radical extension forces a [solvable](c:solvable-group) Galois group.
steps.detail: Adjoin the needed [roots of unity](c:root-of-unity) first and then the radicals one at a time; in characteristic $0$ each step is Galois with abelian group. So the Galois closure of the tower has a solvable group, and the Galois group of the irreducible polynomial is a quotient of it, hence solvable.

steps.slogan: Show that $S_n$ is not solvable for $n \ge 5$ with commutators of $3$-cycles.
steps.detail: With distinct letters $a, b, c, d, e$, the $3$-cycle $(a\,b\,c)$ equals the commutator $[(a\,b\,d), (a\,c\,e)]$. So each term of the [derived series](c:derived-series) contains all $3$-cycles, the series never reaches $\{1\}$, and $S_n$ is not solvable.

steps.slogan: Combine the three steps to exclude a root by radicals.
steps.detail: The general polynomial is irreducible over $K(t)$ because $S_n$ permutes its roots transitively. A root in a radical extension would make $S_n$ solvable by step 2, which step 3 excludes for $n \ge 5$.

concepts.c:field: The base field and its characteristic set the frame of the radical extensions.
concepts.c:galois-group: The Galois group $S_n$ is the invariant that blocks a formula by radicals.
concepts.c:symmetric-group: The full symmetric group acts on the roots of the general polynomial.
concepts.c:elementary-symmetric-polynomial: Elementary symmetric polynomials play the role of the indeterminate coefficients.
concepts.c:solvable-group: Radical towers produce solvable groups, and S_n is not solvable.
concepts.c:root-of-unity: Adjoined roots of unity make each radical step abelian.
concepts.c:derived-series: All 3-cycles stay in every derived subgroup, so the series never ends.

statement: Let $\mathcal{C}$ be a [complete](c:complete-category), [locally small](c:locally-small) category and $G\colon \mathcal{C} \to \mathcal{D}$ a functor that preserves all small [limits](c:limit-category-theory) and satisfies the [solution set condition](c:solution-set-condition). Then $G$ has a [left adjoint](c:adjoint-functor) $F$, with natural bijections $\mathcal{C}(Fd, c) \cong \mathcal{D}(d, Gc)$.

hypotheses.text: The category $\mathcal{C}$ is [complete](c:complete-category) and [locally small](c:locally-small).
The functor $G$ preserves all small [limits](c:limit-category-theory).
For each object $d$ of $\mathcal{D}$, a set of arrows $f_i\colon d \to Gc_i$ exists such that every arrow $d \to Gc$ equals $G(t) \circ f_i$ for some $i$ and $t$.

proofs.name: Initial objects of comma categories
proofs.slogan: For each object $d$, build an initial object of the comma category $d \downarrow G$ from the solution set, and assemble these universal arrows into a left adjoint.
proofs.scope: The existence of the left adjoint. The converse, that a right adjoint preserves limits and has a solution set, is a separate fact.

roles.why: Completeness and small hom-sets give products of sets of objects and the equalizer of all endomorphisms of one object.
Preservation of limits lifts limits of $\mathcal{C}$ to the [comma category](c:comma) $d \downarrow G$.
The solution set is a set of objects of $d \downarrow G$ that maps to every object.

steps.slogan: Show that the [comma category](c:comma) $d \downarrow G$ is complete with small hom-sets.
steps.detail: Objects are pairs $(c, f\colon d \to Gc)$. For a small diagram $(c_j, f_j)$ take $c = \lim c_j$; since $G$ preserves this limit, the cone $(f_j)$ gives a unique $f\colon d \to Gc$, and $(c, f)$ is the limit. Hom-sets are subsets of hom-sets of $\mathcal{C}$.

steps.slogan: Take the product of the solution set to get a [weakly initial object](c:weakly-initial-object) $W$.
steps.detail: The solution set $\{(c_i, f_i)\}$ is a set, so it has a product $W$ in $d \downarrow G$ by step 1. Every object receives an arrow from some $(c_i, f_i)$, hence from $W$ through a projection.

steps.slogan: Equalize all endomorphisms of $W$ to get an [initial object](c:initial-object) $(Fd, \eta_d)$.
steps.detail: The endomorphisms of $W$ form a set; let $e\colon E \to W$ be their joint equalizer, so $E$ is weakly initial. For $u, v\colon E \to X$ with equalizer $k$, choose $s\colon W \to \mathrm{dom}\,k$; then $e k s e = e$, so $k s e = 1_E$ because $e$ is monic, and $u = uk se = vkse = v$.

steps.slogan: Assemble the universal arrows $\eta_d$ into a left adjoint $F$.
steps.detail: An initial object $(Fd, \eta_d)$ of $d \downarrow G$ is a universal arrow: every $h\colon d \to Gc$ equals $G(t)\eta_d$ for a unique $t\colon Fd \to c$. This defines $F$ on arrows and gives the natural bijection $\mathcal{C}(Fd, c) \cong \mathcal{D}(d, Gc)$ of an [adjunction](c:adjoint-functor).

concepts.c:complete-category: Completeness of the category supplies the products and equalizers used.
concepts.c:locally-small: Small hom-sets make the endomorphisms of W a set.
concepts.c:limit-category-theory: Limits in the comma category come from limits preserved by G.
concepts.c:solution-set-condition: The solution set condition reduces a proper class of arrows to a set.
concepts.c:adjoint-functor: The left adjoint is assembled from universal arrows.
concepts.c:comma: Initial objects of $d \downarrow G$ are exactly the universal arrows.
concepts.c:weakly-initial-object: A weakly initial object is the first approximation to an initial object.
concepts.c:initial-object: The initial object gives the value of the left adjoint at d.

source.note: Freyd's proof, as in S. Mac Lane, Categories for the Working Mathematician, section V.6.

statement: If $(a_n)_{n \ge 0}$ is a nonincreasing [monotone sequence](c:monotone-sequence) of real numbers with [limit](c:limit-of-a-sequence) $0$, then the [alternating series](c:alternating-series) $\sum_{n \ge 0} (-1)^n a_n$ converges.

hypotheses.text: The sequence is nonincreasing: $a_{n+1} \le a_n$ for every $n$.
The terms tend to zero: $a_n \to 0$.

conclusion: The [partial sums](c:partial-sum) $S_N = \sum_{n<N} (-1)^n a_n$ converge to a real number.

proofs.name: Summation by parts
proofs.slogan: The partial sums of $(-1)^n$ are bounded by $1$, so summation by parts turns the series into a boundary term and an absolutely convergent series.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem. Nonnegativity of the $a_n$ follows from the hypotheses and is not assumed.

roles.why: Monotonicity makes the differences $a_n - a_{n+1}$ nonnegative, so their sum telescopes.
The limit $0$ kills the boundary term and makes the telescoped sum converge.

steps.slogan: Bound the [partial sums](c:partial-sum) $B_N = \sum_{n<N} (-1)^n$ by $1$.
steps.detail: The sums $B_N$ alternate between $0$ and $1$, so $|B_N| \le 1$ for every $N$.

steps.slogan: Rewrite the partial sums $S_N$ by summation by parts.
steps.detail: Abel's lemma with $f_n = a_n$ and $g_n = (-1)^n$ gives $S_N = a_{N-1} B_N - \sum_{n=0}^{N-2} (a_{n+1} - a_n) B_{n+1}$ for $N \ge 1$.

steps.slogan: Show that the boundary term $a_{N-1} B_N$ tends to $0$.
steps.detail: Step 1 gives $|a_{N-1} B_N| \le |a_{N-1}|$, and $a_{N-1} \to 0$ by hypothesis, so the boundary term tends to $0$.

steps.slogan: Show that $\sum (a_{n+1} - a_n) B_{n+1}$ converges absolutely by telescoping.
steps.detail: Since the sequence is nonincreasing, $|(a_{n+1} - a_n) B_{n+1}| \le a_n - a_{n+1}$, and $\sum_{n<N} (a_n - a_{n+1}) = a_0 - a_N \to a_0$. A series dominated by a convergent series of nonnegative terms has [Cauchy](c:cauchy-sequence) partial sums, so it converges.

steps.slogan: Combine the boundary term and the convergent series to get convergence of $S_N$.
steps.detail: By step 2, $S_N$ is the boundary term minus a partial sum of the series of step 4. Both converge by steps 3 and 4, so $S_N$ converges in $\mathbb{R}$; this is Dirichlet's test for $(-1)^n$.

concepts.c:monotone-sequence: Monotonicity gives nonnegative differences that telescope.
concepts.c:limit-of-a-sequence: The limit zero removes the boundary term and closes the telescope.
concepts.c:alternating-series: The alternating signs have bounded partial sums.
concepts.c:partial-sum: Bounded partial sums of $(-1)^n$ feed summation by parts.
concepts.c:cauchy-sequence: Absolute convergence is shown through Cauchy partial sums and completeness.

proofs.name: Even and odd partial sums
proofs.slogan: The even partial sums increase, the odd ones decrease, every even sum lies below every odd sum, and their gap tends to zero.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem. The proof also gives the error bound $|S - S_N| \le a_N$.

roles.why: Monotonicity makes the even sums increase and the odd sums decrease, and with the limit it gives $a_n \ge 0$.
The limit $0$ gives $a_n \ge 0$ and closes the gap $S_{2k+1} - S_{2k} = a_{2k}$.

steps.slogan: Show that every term $a_n$ is nonnegative.
steps.detail: For $m \ge n$ the [monotone sequence](c:monotone-sequence) gives $a_m \le a_n$; letting $m \to \infty$ gives $0 \le a_n$.

steps.slogan: Show that the even partial sums increase and the odd partial sums decrease.
steps.detail: $S_{2k+2} - S_{2k} = a_{2k} - a_{2k+1} \ge 0$ and $S_{2k+3} - S_{2k+1} = a_{2k+2} - a_{2k+1} \le 0$, because the sequence is nonincreasing.

steps.slogan: Check that every even partial sum lies below every odd partial sum.
steps.detail: $S_{2k+1} - S_{2k} = a_{2k} \ge 0$ by step 1. With $l = \max(j, k)$, step 2 gives $S_{2j} \le S_{2l} \le S_{2l+1} \le S_{2k+1}$.

steps.slogan: Take the limits of the two bounded monotone sequences and close the gap.
steps.detail: The even sums increase and are bounded by $S_1$, the odd sums decrease and are bounded below by $S_0$, so both converge. Their limits differ by $\lim a_{2k} = 0$, so all [partial sums](c:partial-sum) converge to one limit.

concepts.c:monotone-sequence: Monotone bounded sequences of partial sums converge.
concepts.c:limit-of-a-sequence: The limit zero makes the two limits of partial sums coincide.
concepts.c:alternating-series: Alternating signs make the even and odd sums move in opposite directions.
concepts.c:partial-sum: The proof splits the partial sums into even and odd ones.

source.note: Leibniz's classical argument with even and odd partial sums.

statement: Let $g\colon \mathbb{R}^d \to E$ be a measurable function into a [Banach space](c:banach-space), [continuous](c:continuous-function) at $x_0$. Let $\varphi_k \ge 0$ be [mollifiers](c:mollifier) with $\int \varphi_k = 1$ that vanish outside the ball of radius $r_k$, where $r_k \to 0$. If $x_k \to x_0$, then the [convolutions](c:convolution) satisfy $(\varphi_k * g)(x_k) \to g(x_0)$.

hypotheses.text: The function $g\colon \mathbb{R}^d \to E$ is measurable, and $E$ is a [Banach space](c:banach-space).
The function $g$ is [continuous](c:continuous-function) at $x_0$.
Each $\varphi_k$ is nonnegative with integral $1$ and vanishes outside the ball of radius $r_k$ about $0$, where $r_k \to 0$.
The points satisfy $x_k \to x_0$.

conclusion: The values $(\varphi_k * g)(x_k) = \int \varphi_k(t)\, g(x_k - t)\,dt$ tend to $g(x_0)$.

formal.difference: The declaration works on a finite-dimensional real normed space with an additive Haar measure, along any filter, with mathlib's normed smooth bump functions. It also lets the function g_i vary with i, provided g_i(x) tends to z_0 jointly in i and x.

proofs.name: Weighted average near the point
proofs.slogan: Write the convolution minus $g(x_0)$ as an average of $g(x_k - t) - g(x_0)$ over a shrinking ball, where continuity makes it small.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem. The convolution may be undefined for small $k$, and the proof uses only large $k$.

roles.why: Measurability makes the integrand measurable, and completeness of $E$ gives the Bochner integral.
Continuity at $x_0$ makes $g(y) - g(x_0)$ small and $g$ bounded for $y$ near $x_0$.
Unit mass rewrites the difference as one integral, and nonnegativity with shrinking support bounds it.
The points $x_k$ enter every ball about $x_0$, so $x_k - t$ stays near $x_0$.

steps.slogan: Choose $\delta > 0$ with $\|g(y) - g(x_0)\| < \varepsilon$ whenever $|y - x_0| < \delta$.
steps.detail: Fix $\varepsilon > 0$. [Continuity](c:continuous-function) of $g$ at $x_0$ gives such a $\delta$; in particular $g$ is bounded on the ball $B(x_0, \delta)$.

steps.slogan: Take $k$ so large that $r_k < \delta/2$ and $|x_k - x_0| < \delta/2$.
steps.detail: Both hold for all large $k$ because $r_k \to 0$ and $x_k \to x_0$. Then $\varphi_k(t) \ne 0$ forces $|t| < \delta/2$, so $|x_k - t - x_0| < \delta$.

steps.slogan: Check that the [convolution](c:convolution) integral exists for these large $k$.
steps.detail: The integrand $t \mapsto \varphi_k(t)\, g(x_k - t)$ is measurable, vanishes outside a bounded ball, and is bounded there by steps 1 and 2, so it is integrable.

steps.slogan: Subtract $g(x_0)$ inside the integral with the unit mass of $\varphi_k$.
steps.detail: Since $\int \varphi_k = 1$, the constant $g(x_0)$ equals $\int \varphi_k(t)\, g(x_0)\,dt$. Hence $(\varphi_k * g)(x_k) - g(x_0) = \int \varphi_k(t)\big(g(x_k - t) - g(x_0)\big)\,dt$.

steps.slogan: Bound the rewritten integral by $\varepsilon$ with the nonnegative weights of the [mollifier](c:mollifier).
steps.detail: On the support of $\varphi_k$ the factor $\|g(x_k - t) - g(x_0)\|$ is below $\varepsilon$ by steps 1 and 2. As $\varphi_k \ge 0$ has integral $1$, the norm of the integral is at most $\varepsilon$ for all large $k$.

concepts.c:banach-space: Completeness of the target space makes the vector-valued integral exist.
concepts.c:continuous-function: Continuity at $x_0$ is the only regularity the proof needs.
concepts.c:mollifier: The mollifier is a nonnegative unit-mass weight with shrinking support.
concepts.c:convolution: The convolution is a weighted average of nearby values of g.

statement: Let there be at least three alternatives and finitely many voters, each with a strict ranking. If a [social welfare function](c:social-welfare-function) turns every profile of rankings into a complete transitive social [preference](c:preference-relation) and satisfies unanimity and independence of irrelevant alternatives, then it is a dictatorship: one voter's strict preferences always become strict social preferences.

hypotheses.text: There are at least three alternatives.
The set of voters is finite and nonempty.
Every profile of strict rankings is allowed, and the social [preference](c:preference-relation) is complete and transitive.
If every voter ranks $a$ above $b$, then society ranks $a$ strictly above $b$ ([Pareto](c:pareto-efficiency) unanimity).
The social ranking of $a$ and $b$ depends only on the voters' rankings of $a$ and $b$.

conclusion: Some voter $n^*$ is a dictator: whenever $n^*$ ranks $a$ above $b$, society ranks $a$ strictly above $b$.

proofs.name: Pivotal voter
proofs.slogan: Move one alternative from bottom to top voter by voter, find the voter at whom society's ranking flips, and show that this voter dictates.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem, after Geanakoplos's first proof. With one voter the dictator is that voter.

roles.why: A third alternative is needed to compare two others through it and to run the argument twice.
Finitely many voters can be moved one at a time, so a first flipping voter exists.
Every modified profile is admissible, and transitivity of the social preference drives each comparison.
Unanimity fixes the social position of $b$ at the start and at the end of the sweep.
Independence transfers social comparisons between profiles that agree on a pair.

steps.slogan: Show that society puts $b$ first or last when every voter does.
steps.detail: Suppose society has $a \succeq b \succeq c$ for some $a, c \ne b$. Moving $c$ just above $a$ for every voter keeps each voter's $a$–$b$ and $b$–$c$ comparisons, so independence keeps $a \succeq b \succeq c$ and transitivity gives $a \succeq c$, while unanimity gives $c \succ a$.

steps.slogan: Move $b$ from bottom to top one voter at a time and find the pivotal voter $n^*$.
steps.detail: When all voters rank $b$ last, unanimity puts $b$ socially last; when all rank it first, socially first. By step 1, $b$ stays socially extreme, so a first voter $n^*$ exists whose move takes $b$ from the social bottom to the social top.

steps.slogan: Show that $n^*$ dictates every pair $a, c$ that does not involve $b$.
steps.detail: Let $n^*$ rank $a$ over $c$, move $b$ between them for $n^*$, to the top for earlier voters and to the bottom for later ones. Independence gives $a \succ b$ as just before the flip and $b \succ c$ as just after it, so $a \succ c$, and independence carries this to every profile where $n^*$ ranks $a$ over $c$.

steps.slogan: Show that $n^*$ also dictates the pairs that involve $b$.
steps.detail: Steps 2 and 3 with a third alternative $c$ in place of $b$ give a voter who dictates every pair without $c$, such as $a, b$. In the two profiles around the flip of step 2, only $n^*$ changes a ranking, yet the social ranking of $a$ and $b$ changes, so that voter is $n^*$.

steps.slogan: Combine the two cases to conclude that $n^*$ is a dictator.
steps.detail: Steps 3 and 4 cover every pair of distinct alternatives. So whenever $n^*$ ranks $a$ above $b$, the [social welfare function](c:social-welfare-function) ranks $a$ strictly above $b$.

concepts.c:social-welfare-function: The rule that aggregates rankings is the object shown to be dictatorial.
concepts.c:preference-relation: Transitivity of social preference produces each contradiction and comparison.
concepts.c:pareto-efficiency: Unanimity pins the social position of b at both ends of the sweep.

source.note: The pivotal-voter proof of J. Geanakoplos, Three brief proofs of Arrow's impossibility theorem, Economic Theory 26 (2005), 211-215.

statement: Over a field $k$, let $C$ be a coaugmented conilpotent dg [coalgebra](c:coalgebra) and $A$ an augmented [dg algebra](c:differential-graded-algebra). There are natural bijections $\mathrm{Hom}(\Omega C, A) \cong \mathrm{Tw}(C, A) \cong \mathrm{Hom}(C, BA)$, where $\mathrm{Tw}(C, A)$ is the set of [twisting morphisms](c:twisting-cochain). So the cobar construction $\Omega$ is left [adjoint](c:adjoint-functor) to the bar construction $B$.

hypotheses.text: The ground ring $k$ is a field.
$C$ is a coaugmented dg [coalgebra](c:coalgebra) whose coradical filtration is exhaustive, that is, conilpotent.
$A$ is an [augmented](c:augmented-algebra) dg algebra.

conclusion: Dg algebra maps $\Omega C \to A$, twisting morphisms $C \to A$ and dg coalgebra maps $C \to BA$ correspond bijectively and naturally in $C$ and $A$.

proofs.name: Twisting morphisms as the middle term
proofs.slogan: Maps out of the free algebra $\Omega C$ and into the cofree coalgebra $BA$ are both fixed by one degree $-1$ map, and both differential conditions become the Maurer-Cartan equation.
proofs.scope: The adjunction and its natural bijections. That the counit $\Omega B A \to A$ is a quasi-isomorphism is a further theorem not proved here.

roles.why: Over a field the tensor algebra is free and the tensor coalgebra is cofree among conilpotent coalgebras.
The coproduct gives the differential of $\Omega C$, and conilpotency makes maps into $T^c(s\bar A)$ determined by one projection.
The augmentation splits off $\bar A$, and the product gives the differential of $BA$.

steps.slogan: Define $\Omega C$ and $BA$ on [tensor algebras](c:tensor-algebra) with two-part differentials.
steps.detail: Set $\Omega C = (T(s^{-1}\bar C), d_1 + d_2)$, with $d_1$ from $d_C$ and $d_2$ from the reduced coproduct, extended as derivations. Dually $BA = (T^c(s\bar A), d_1 + d_2)$ with $d_2$ from the product of $\bar A$, extended as coderivations; coassociativity and associativity give $d^2 = 0$.

steps.slogan: Identify graded algebra maps $\Omega C \to A$ with degree $-1$ maps $\alpha\colon \bar C \to \bar A$.
steps.detail: A morphism of augmented graded algebras out of the free algebra $T(s^{-1}\bar C)$ is fixed by its values on generators. These form a degree $0$ map $s^{-1}\bar C \to \bar A$, that is, a degree $-1$ map $\alpha$, extended by $0$ to $C \to A$.

steps.slogan: Show that the algebra map commutes with the differentials iff $\partial\alpha + \alpha \star \alpha = 0$.
steps.detail: Both $f \circ d_{\Omega C}$ and $d_A \circ f$ are derivations along $f$, so they agree iff they agree on generators. There $d_1$ gives $\partial\alpha$ and $d_2$ gives $\alpha \star \alpha = \mu(\alpha \otimes \alpha)\Delta$, which yields the [Maurer-Cartan equation](c:maurer-cartan-equation) defining a twisting morphism.

steps.slogan: Identify dg coalgebra maps $C \to BA$ with twisting morphisms in the dual way.
steps.detail: Because $C$ is conilpotent, a coalgebra map $C \to T^c(s\bar A)$ is fixed by its projection to $s\bar A$, again a degree $-1$ map $\alpha$. Comparing coderivations on cogenerators shows that it commutes with the differentials iff $\partial\alpha + \alpha \star \alpha = 0$.

steps.slogan: Check that both bijections are natural in $C$ and $A$, which gives the adjunction.
steps.detail: A coalgebra map $C' \to C$ or an algebra map $A \to A'$ acts on all three sets by composition, and the bijections commute with these actions. Natural bijections $\mathrm{Hom}(\Omega C, A) \cong \mathrm{Hom}(C, BA)$ form an [adjunction](c:adjoint-functor) $\Omega \dashv B$.

concepts.c:coalgebra: The cobar construction starts from a conilpotent dg coalgebra.
concepts.c:differential-graded-algebra: The bar construction starts from an augmented dg algebra.
concepts.c:twisting-cochain: Twisting morphisms are the middle term of both bijections.
concepts.c:adjoint-functor: Natural bijections of hom-sets are exactly an adjunction.
concepts.c:augmented-algebra: The augmentation splits off the ideal $\bar A$ that generates $BA$.
concepts.c:tensor-algebra: Both constructions are tensor (co)algebras with extra differentials.
concepts.c:maurer-cartan-equation: Both differential conditions reduce to the Maurer-Cartan equation.

source.note: The standard proof in J.-L. Loday and B. Vallette, Algebraic Operads, Springer 2012, section 2.2.

statement: Every [closed subgroup](c:closed-subgroup) $H$ of a finite-dimensional [Lie group](c:lie-group) $G$ is an embedded [submanifold](c:submanifold) of $G$. With this smooth structure $H$ is a Lie group whose [Lie algebra](c:lie-algebra) is $\mathfrak{h} = \{X \in \mathfrak{g} : \exp(tX) \in H \text{ for all } t \in \mathbb{R}\}$.

hypotheses.text: $G$ is a finite-dimensional [Lie group](c:lie-group) with Lie algebra $\mathfrak{g}$.
$H$ is a subgroup of $G$.
$H$ is a closed subset of $G$.

conclusion: $H$ is an embedded Lie subgroup of $G$ with Lie algebra $\mathfrak{h}$.

proofs.name: Exponential slice chart
proofs.slogan: Show that $\mathfrak{h}$ is a subspace, use the exponential map to build a slice chart of $H$ near the identity, and translate it.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem, including discrete $H$ (where $\mathfrak{h} = 0$) and open $H$ (where $\mathfrak{h} = \mathfrak{g}$).

roles.why: Finite dimension gives a compact unit sphere in $\mathfrak{g}$, and smoothness makes $\exp$ a local diffeomorphism.
Powers and products of elements of $H$ stay in $H$, and left translation by $h \in H$ maps $H$ onto $H$.
Closedness keeps limits of points of $H$ inside $H$.

steps.slogan: Show that limit directions of small elements of $H$ lie in $\mathfrak{h}$.
steps.detail: Let $0 \ne X_n \to 0$ with $\exp X_n \in H$ and $X_n/|X_n| \to X$. For $t \in \mathbb{R}$ put $m_n = \lfloor t/|X_n| \rfloor$; then $\exp(m_n X_n) = (\exp X_n)^{m_n} \in H$ and $m_n X_n \to tX$. As $H$ is closed, $\exp(tX) \in H$, so $X \in \mathfrak{h}$.

steps.slogan: Show that $\mathfrak{h}$ is a linear subspace of the [Lie algebra](c:lie-algebra) $\mathfrak{g}$.
steps.detail: The set is closed under scalar multiples by definition. For $X, Y \in \mathfrak{h}$ and $t \neq 0$, $\exp(tX/n)\exp(tY/n) = \exp Z_n$ with $nZ_n \to t(X + Y)$, so if $X + Y \ne 0$, step 1 puts the direction of $X + Y$ in $\mathfrak{h}$, hence $X + Y \in \mathfrak{h}$.

steps.slogan: Show that near the identity $H$ meets an [exponential](c:exponential-map) chart exactly in $\exp$ of a ball of $\mathfrak{h}$.
steps.detail: Write $\mathfrak{g} = \mathfrak{h} \oplus \mathfrak{m}$; then $\Phi(Y, Z) = \exp(Y)\exp(Z)$ is a [local diffeomorphism](c:local-diffeomorphism) at $0$. If $\Phi(Y_n, Z_n) \in H$ tends to $e$ with $Z_n \ne 0$, then $\exp Z_n \in H$, and a limit direction of $Z_n$ is a unit vector of $\mathfrak{m}$ that lies in $\mathfrak{h}$ by step 1, a contradiction.

steps.slogan: Translate the slice chart by left multiplication to every point of $H$.
steps.detail: Step 3 gives a chart around $e$ in which $H$ is the linear slice $\mathfrak{h} \times \{0\}$. Left translation by $h \in H$ is a diffeomorphism of $G$ that maps $H$ onto $H$, so $H$ has slice charts everywhere and is an embedded [submanifold](c:submanifold).

steps.slogan: Restrict the smooth group operations of $G$ to the embedded submanifold $H$.
steps.detail: Multiplication and inversion map $H \times H$ and $H$ into $H$, and a smooth map into $G$ with values in an embedded submanifold is smooth into it. So $H$ is a Lie group, and step 3 shows that its tangent space at $e$ is $\mathfrak{h}$.

concepts.c:closed-subgroup: Closedness is what makes the subgroup a submanifold.
concepts.c:lie-group: The ambient Lie group supplies the exponential map and translations.
concepts.c:submanifold: The theorem shows that H is an embedded submanifold.
concepts.c:lie-algebra: The candidate Lie algebra $\mathfrak{h}$ is a subspace of $\mathfrak{g}$.
concepts.c:exponential-map: The exponential map gives the chart in which H becomes a slice.
concepts.c:local-diffeomorphism: The map $\Phi$ is a chart because it is a local diffeomorphism.

source.note: The standard proof through the exponential map, as in F. W. Warner, Foundations of Differentiable Manifolds and Lie Groups, theorem 3.42.

statement: For all natural numbers $m, n, k$ the [binomial coefficients](c:binomial-coefficient) satisfy $\binom{m+n}{k} = \sum_{j=0}^{k} \binom{m}{j}\binom{n}{k-j}$. Both sides are polynomials in $m$ and $n$, so the identity also holds as the [polynomial identity](c:polynomial-identity) $\binom{x+y}{k} = \sum_{j=0}^{k}\binom{x}{j}\binom{y}{k-j}$, where $\binom{x}{j} = x(x-1)\cdots(x-j+1)/j!$.

hypotheses.text: The lower index $k$ is a natural number.
The upper indices $m, n$ are natural numbers, or, in the polynomial form, $x$ and $y$ are indeterminates over $\mathbb{Q}$.

conclusion: $\binom{m+n}{k} = \sum_{j=0}^{k}\binom{m}{j}\binom{n}{k-j}$ for natural $m, n$, and the same identity holds in $\mathbb{Q}[x, y]$.

proofs.name: Coefficients of a product
proofs.slogan: Compare the coefficients of $t^k$ in $(1+t)^{m+n} = (1+t)^m(1+t)^n$, then extend from natural numbers to polynomials.
proofs.scope: Natural numbers first, then the polynomial form. The convention $\binom{m}{j} = 0$ for $j > m$ keeps the sum correct when $k$ exceeds $m$ or $n$.

roles.why: Each natural $k$ indexes a coefficient of the polynomial $(1+t)^{m+n}$.
Natural exponents give polynomial expansions, and infinitely many natural values force the polynomial form.

steps.slogan: Expand $(1+t)^m$, $(1+t)^n$ and $(1+t)^{m+n}$ by the binomial theorem.
steps.detail: The binomial theorem gives $(1+t)^m = \sum_j \binom{m}{j} t^j$ with [binomial coefficients](c:binomial-coefficient) $\binom{m}{j} = 0$ for $j > m$, and in the same way for $n$ and for $m + n$.

steps.slogan: Compare the coefficients of $t^k$ on both sides of $(1+t)^{m+n} = (1+t)^m(1+t)^n$.
steps.detail: The coefficient of $t^k$ on the left is $\binom{m+n}{k}$. On the right, the $k$-th coefficient of a product of two polynomials is $\sum_{j=0}^{k} \binom{m}{j}\binom{n}{k-j}$. Equal polynomials have equal coefficients.

steps.slogan: Extend the identity from natural numbers to the [polynomial ring](c:polynomial-ring) $\mathbb{Q}[x, y]$.
steps.detail: The difference $D(x, y) = \binom{x+y}{k} - \sum_j \binom{x}{j}\binom{y}{k-j}$ is a polynomial that vanishes on $\mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{N}$. For each fixed $n \in \mathbb{N}$, $D(x, n)$ has infinitely many roots, so it is zero; then each coefficient of $D$ in $x$ is a polynomial in $y$ with infinitely many roots, so $D = 0$.

concepts.c:binomial-coefficient: Binomial coefficients are the coefficients of the powers of 1 + t.
concepts.c:polynomial-identity: The final step lifts the numerical identity to a polynomial identity.
concepts.c:polynomial-ring: The identity is extended into the ring of polynomials in x and y.

source.note: The standard generating-polynomial proof by comparison of coefficients.

proofs.name: Choosing a committee
proofs.slogan: Count the $k$-element subsets of the union of an $m$-set and an $n$-set by how many elements they take from the first set.
proofs.scope: Natural numbers by counting, then the polynomial form by the same extension step as in the first proof.

roles.why: The subsets counted have exactly $k$ elements.
Natural $m$ and $n$ are sizes of finite sets, and infinitely many values force the polynomial form.

steps.slogan: Count the $k$-subsets of a disjoint union $M \sqcup N$ with $|M| = m$ and $|N| = n$.
steps.detail: The union has $m + n$ elements, and a [binomial coefficient](c:binomial-coefficient) counts the subsets of a given size, so there are $\binom{m+n}{k}$ subsets of size $k$.

steps.slogan: Sort the $k$-subsets by the number $j$ of their elements in $M$.
steps.detail: A $k$-subset $S$ corresponds bijectively to the pair $(S \cap M, S \cap N)$ of a $j$-subset of $M$ and a $(k-j)$-subset of $N$, for one $j$ with $0 \le j \le k$. So $\binom{m}{j}\binom{n}{k-j}$ subsets have this $j$, and the sum over $j$ is the right side.

steps.slogan: Extend the identity from natural numbers to the [polynomial ring](c:polynomial-ring) $\mathbb{Q}[x, y]$.
steps.detail: The difference $D(x, y) = \binom{x+y}{k} - \sum_j \binom{x}{j}\binom{y}{k-j}$ is a polynomial that vanishes on $\mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{N}$. For each fixed $n \in \mathbb{N}$, $D(x, n)$ has infinitely many roots, so it is zero; then each coefficient of $D$ in $x$ is a polynomial in $y$ with infinitely many roots, so $D = 0$.

concepts.c:binomial-coefficient: Binomial coefficients count subsets of a given size.
concepts.c:polynomial-identity: The counting identity is lifted to a polynomial identity at the end.
concepts.c:polynomial-ring: The identity is extended into the ring of polynomials in x and y.

source.note: The standard double-counting proof, choosing a committee of k from m women and n men.

statement: Let $Z \subseteq \mathbb{R}^m$ be nonempty and [compact](c:compact-space), and let $\phi\colon \mathbb{R}^n \times Z \to \mathbb{R}$ be [continuous](c:continuous-function) with partial gradient $\nabla_x\phi$ existing and continuous. Then $f(x) = \max_{z \in Z} \phi(x, z)$ has a [directional derivative](c:directional-derivative) in every direction $y$, namely $f'(x; y) = \max_{z \in Z_0(x)} \nabla_x\phi(x, z) \cdot y$, with $Z_0(x)$ the set of maximizers.

hypotheses.text: The set $Z \subseteq \mathbb{R}^m$ is nonempty and [compact](c:compact-space).
The function $\phi$ is [continuous](c:continuous-function) on $\mathbb{R}^n \times Z$.
The partial gradient $\nabla_x\phi(x, z)$ exists and is continuous on $\mathbb{R}^n \times Z$.

conclusion: For all $x$ and $y$ the limit $f'(x; y) = \lim_{t \to 0^+} (f(x + ty) - f(x))/t$ exists and equals $\max_{z \in Z_0(x)} \nabla_x\phi(x, z) \cdot y$.

proofs.name: Lower and upper bounds
proofs.slogan: Bound the difference quotient below with a fixed maximizer, and above with maximizers at the moved points and the mean value theorem.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem for each fixed $x$ and $y$. If $Z_0(x) = \{z\}$, it gives $f'(x; y) = \nabla_x\phi(x, z) \cdot y$, so $f$ is differentiable at $x$.

roles.why: Compactness makes each maximum attained and gives convergent subsequences of maximizers.
Continuity of $\phi$ makes the maximum exist and makes limits of maximizers maximizers.
The gradient gives the slope along $y$ for fixed $z$, and its joint continuity controls the mean value points.

steps.slogan: Show that the maximum defining $f$ is attained on a nonempty compact set $Z_0(x)$.
steps.detail: For fixed $x$, $z \mapsto \phi(x, z)$ is continuous on the nonempty [compact](c:compact-space) set $Z$, so it attains its maximum. The set $Z_0(x)$ of maximizers is closed in $Z$, hence compact and nonempty.

steps.slogan: Bound the difference quotient below with a fixed maximizer $z \in Z_0(x)$.
steps.detail: For $t > 0$, $f(x + ty) - f(x) \ge \phi(x + ty, z) - \phi(x, z)$. Dividing by $t$ and letting $t \to 0^+$ gives $\liminf (f(x + ty) - f(x))/t \ge \nabla_x\phi(x, z) \cdot y$ for every $z \in Z_0(x)$.

steps.slogan: Bound the difference quotient above with maximizers $z_t \in Z_0(x + ty)$ and the mean value theorem.
steps.detail: Since $f(x) \ge \phi(x, z_t)$, we get $f(x + ty) - f(x) \le \phi(x + ty, z_t) - \phi(x, z_t) = t\,\nabla_x\phi(x + \theta_t t y, z_t) \cdot y$ for some $\theta_t \in (0, 1)$.

steps.slogan: Pass to a convergent subsequence of maximizers and show that its limit maximizes at $x$.
steps.detail: Take $t_k \to 0^+$ that realizes the limsup and a subsequence with $z_{t_k} \to \bar z$. From $\phi(x + t_k y, z_{t_k}) \ge \phi(x + t_k y, z)$ for all $z$, continuity gives $\bar z \in Z_0(x)$, and joint continuity of $\nabla_x\phi$ gives $\limsup \le \nabla_x\phi(x, \bar z) \cdot y$.

steps.slogan: Combine the two bounds into the formula for the [directional derivative](c:directional-derivative).
steps.detail: Steps 2 and 4 give $\max_{Z_0(x)} \nabla_x\phi(x, z) \cdot y \le \liminf \le \limsup \le \max_{Z_0(x)} \nabla_x\phi(x, z) \cdot y$, where the maximum exists because $Z_0(x)$ is compact. So the limit exists and equals the maximum.

concepts.c:compact-space: Compactness gives maximizers and convergent subsequences of maximizers.
concepts.c:continuous-function: Continuity of phi makes limits of maximizers maximizers.
concepts.c:directional-derivative: The theorem computes the one-sided directional derivative of the maximum.

source.note: The standard two-sided estimate, as in D. P. Bertsekas, Nonlinear Programming, appendix B (Danskin's theorem); the result is due to J. M. Danskin (1966).

statement: Let $E, F$ be [normed spaces](c:normed-space) over $\mathbb{R}$, $\mathbb{C}$ or another nontrivially normed field, with $f\colon F \to E$, $g\colon E \to F$ and $a \in E$. If $g$ is continuous at $a$, $f$ has [derivative](c:frechet-derivative) $f'$ at $g(a)$ that is a [continuous linear equivalence](c:continuous-linear-equivalence), and $f(g(y)) = y$ near $a$, then $g$ has derivative $(f')^{-1}$ at $a$.

hypotheses.text: The map $g$ is continuous at $a$.
The map $f$ has [derivative](c:frechet-derivative) $f'$ at $g(a)$, and $f'\colon F \to E$ is a [continuous linear equivalence](c:continuous-linear-equivalence).
The map $f$ is a left [inverse](c:inverse-function) of $g$ near $a$: $f(g(y)) = y$ for all $y$ in a neighborhood of $a$.

conclusion: The map $g$ is differentiable at $a$ with $g(y) = g(a) + (f')^{-1}(y - a) + o(\|y - a\|)$.

proofs.name: Invert the first-order expansion
proofs.slogan: Insert $g(y)$ into the first-order expansion of $f$, apply $(f')^{-1}$, and show that the error is small compared with $y - a$.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem. No inverse function theorem is needed, because the inverse $g$ is given.

roles.why: Continuity sends $y \to a$ to $g(y) \to g(a)$, so the expansion of $f$ at $g(a)$ applies at $g(y)$.
The derivative gives the expansion of $f$, and the bounded inverse $(f')^{-1}$ converts it.
The identity $f(g(y)) = y$ turns the expansion of $f$ into an equation for $g(y) - g(a)$.

steps.slogan: Insert $g(y)$ into the first-order expansion of $f$ at $b = g(a)$.
steps.detail: Here $f(b) = a$. Because $g(y) \to b$ as $y \to a$, the [derivative](c:frechet-derivative) gives $y - a = f(g(y)) - f(b) = f'(g(y) - b) + r(y)$ with $\|r(y)\| \le \varepsilon(y)\|g(y) - b\|$ and $\varepsilon(y) \to 0$.

steps.slogan: Apply the bounded inverse $(f')^{-1}$ to solve for $g(y) - b$.
steps.detail: Then $g(y) - b = (f')^{-1}(y - a) - (f')^{-1}r(y)$, and $\|(f')^{-1}r(y)\| \le C\varepsilon(y)\|g(y) - b\|$ with $C = \|(f')^{-1}\|$, finite because $f'$ is a [continuous linear equivalence](c:continuous-linear-equivalence).

steps.slogan: Bound $\|g(y) - b\|$ by a constant times $\|y - a\|$ near $a$.
steps.detail: For $y$ so close to $a$ that $C\varepsilon(y) \le 1/2$, step 2 gives $\|g(y) - b\| \le C\|y - a\| + \tfrac12\|g(y) - b\|$, so $\|g(y) - b\| \le 2C\|y - a\|$.

steps.slogan: Show that the error is $o(\|y - a\|)$, so $(f')^{-1}$ is the derivative of $g$.
steps.detail: Steps 2 and 3 give $\|g(y) - b - (f')^{-1}(y - a)\| \le 2C^2\varepsilon(y)\|y - a\|$ with $\varepsilon(y) \to 0$. This is the definition of the derivative of the [inverse](c:inverse-function) map $g$ at $a$.

statement: If $q \ge 1$ and $a$ are integers with $\gcd(a, q) = 1$, then there are infinitely many [prime numbers](c:prime-number) $p$ with $p \equiv a$ [modulo](c:modular-arithmetic) $q$.

hypotheses.text: The modulus $q$ is a positive integer.
The residue $a$ is coprime to $q$, so it is a unit [modulo](c:modular-arithmetic) $q$.

conclusion: The set of primes $p$ with $p \equiv a \pmod q$ is infinite.

proofs.name: Dirichlet L-functions at s = 1
proofs.slogan: Isolate the residue class with Dirichlet characters, and show that its sum of $\Lambda(n)/n^s$ has a pole at $s = 1$ because $L(1, \chi) \neq 0$ for $\chi \neq \chi_0$.
proofs.scope: An outline of the mathlib proof. Step 3, the nonvanishing of $L(1, \chi)$, is a substantial theorem that the step only sketches.

roles.why: A positive modulus gives the finite group $(\mathbb{Z}/q\mathbb{Z})^\times$ of order $\varphi(q)$ and its characters.
Characters isolate only a unit class, with weight $1/\varphi(q)$; a non-unit class holds at most one prime.

steps.slogan: Isolate the residue class of $a$ with the orthogonality of [Dirichlet characters](c:dirichlet-character).
steps.detail: For a unit $a$, $\mathbf{1}_{n \equiv a} = \varphi(q)^{-1}\sum_\chi \overline{\chi(a)}\chi(n)$ for $n$ coprime to $q$. So for $\mathrm{Re}\, s > 1$, $\sum_{n \equiv a} \Lambda(n) n^{-s} = \varphi(q)^{-1}\sum_\chi \overline{\chi(a)}\,(-L'/L)(s, \chi)$, with $\Lambda$ the von Mangoldt function.

steps.slogan: Find the simple pole of the principal character term at $s = 1$.
steps.detail: For the principal character $\chi_0$, $L(s, \chi_0)$ is the [Riemann zeta function](c:riemann-zeta-function) times finitely many Euler factors, so $-L'/L(s, \chi_0) = 1/(s - 1) + O(1)$ near $s = 1$. This term contributes $\varphi(q)^{-1}/(s - 1)$.

steps.slogan: Show that $L(1, \chi) \neq 0$ for every non-principal character $\chi$.
steps.detail: For quadratic $\chi$, $\zeta(s)L(s, \chi)$ is a Dirichlet series with nonnegative coefficients; a zero at $1$ would make it entire, hence positive on the real line by Landau's theorem, yet it vanishes at $s = -2$. For other $\chi$, $|L(\sigma, \chi_0)^3 L(\sigma, \chi)^4 L(\sigma, \chi^2)| \ge 1$ for $\sigma > 1$ excludes a zero of this [L-function](c:l-function) at $1$.

steps.slogan: Show that $\sum_{p \equiv a} \log p / p^{s}$ tends to infinity as $s \to 1^+$.
steps.detail: By steps 1 to 3 the class sum is $\varphi(q)^{-1}/(s - 1)$ plus a function bounded near $1$, since each $-L'/L(s, \chi)$ with $\chi \ne \chi_0$ is holomorphic there. Prime powers $p^k$ with $k \ge 2$ contribute a bounded amount, so the sum over primes $p \equiv a$ tends to infinity.

steps.slogan: Derive infinitely many primes in the class from the divergence by contradiction.
steps.detail: If only finitely many [primes](c:prime-number) satisfied $p \equiv a \pmod q$, the sum of $\log p / p^s$ over them would stay bounded as $s \to 1^+$. This contradicts step 4, so the set of such primes is infinite.

statement: The [series](c:series) $\sum_p 1/p$ of the reciprocals of all [prime numbers](c:prime-number) $p$ is a [divergent series](c:divergent-series).
conclusion: The partial sums $\sum_{p \le x} 1/p$ tend to infinity as $x \to \infty$.

proofs.name: Erdős's counting argument
proofs.slogan: If the tail of $\sum 1/p$ were below $1/2$, the integers up to $N = 4^{\pi(k)+1}$ could not all be counted.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem, by contradiction. Here $\pi(k)$ is the number of primes below $k$.

steps.slogan: Assume convergence and choose $k$ with $\sum_{p \ge k} 1/p < 1/2$.
steps.detail: If the [series](c:series) converged, its tails would tend to $0$, so some $k$ has $\sum_{p \ge k} 1/p < 1/2$. Let $\pi(k)$ be the number of primes below $k$ and $N = 4^{\pi(k)+1}$.

steps.slogan: Count the integers up to $N$ whose prime factors all lie below $k$.
steps.detail: Each such $n$ is $m^2 r$ with $r$ a [squarefree integer](c:squarefree-integer) built from the $\pi(k)$ small primes, so $r$ takes at most $2^{\pi(k)}$ values. Since $m \le \sqrt N = 2^{\pi(k)+1}$, there are at most $2^{\pi(k)}\sqrt N = N/2$ such $n$.

steps.slogan: Count the integers up to $N$ that have a prime factor $p \ge k$.
steps.detail: A prime $p$ divides $\lfloor N/p \rfloor \le N/p$ integers in $[1, N]$. So at most $\sum_{p \ge k} N/p < N/2$ of these integers have a prime factor $p \ge k$.

steps.slogan: Add the two counts and contradict the total of $N$ integers.
steps.detail: Every integer in $[1, N]$ falls under step 2 or step 3, so $N < N/2 + N/2 = N$, a contradiction. Hence the series of prime reciprocals diverges.

concepts.c:series: A convergent series has small tails, which the proof contradicts.
concepts.c:prime-number: Integers are sorted by the sizes of their prime factors.
concepts.c:divergent-series: Divergence is reached by refuting convergence.
concepts.c:squarefree-integer: Squarefree parts of smooth numbers have few possible values.

proofs.name: Euler product and the harmonic series
proofs.slogan: Compare the harmonic sum with the Euler product over primes and take logarithms to get $\sum_{p \le x} 1/p > \log\log x - 1$.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem with an explicit lower bound for $x \ge 2$.

steps.slogan: Bound the harmonic sum up to $x$ by the [Euler product](c:euler-product) over primes $p \le x$.
steps.detail: Expanding $\prod_{p \le x}(1 - 1/p)^{-1} = \prod_{p \le x}\sum_{j \ge 0} p^{-j}$ gives $\sum 1/n$ over all $n$ whose prime factors are at most $x$, each $n$ once by unique factorization. Every $n \le x$ is such an $n$, so $\sum_{n \le x} 1/n \le \prod_{p \le x}(1 - 1/p)^{-1}$.

steps.slogan: Bound the harmonic sum up to $x$ below by $\log x$.
steps.detail: Since $1/n \ge \int_n^{n+1} dt/t$, we get $\sum_{n \le x} 1/n \ge \log(\lfloor x \rfloor + 1) \ge \log x$, the quantitative divergence of the [harmonic series](c:harmonic-series).

steps.slogan: Take logarithms and bound each $-\log(1 - 1/p)$ by $1/p + 1/p^2$.
steps.detail: For $0 \le u \le 1/2$, $-\log(1 - u) = \sum_j u^j/j \le u + u^2$. So $\log\log x \le \sum_{p \le x} -\log(1 - 1/p) \le \sum_{p \le x} 1/p + \sum_{n \ge 2} 1/n^2 < \sum_{p \le x} 1/p + 1$.

steps.slogan: Let $x$ tend to infinity in $\sum_{p \le x} 1/p > \log\log x - 1$.
steps.detail: The right side tends to infinity with $x$, so the partial sums of the [series](c:series) over [primes](c:prime-number) are unbounded and the series diverges.

concepts.c:series: The partial sums of the series are bounded below by log log x.
concepts.c:prime-number: Primes index the factors of the Euler product.
concepts.c:divergent-series: Unbounded partial sums of positive terms mean divergence.
concepts.c:euler-product: The Euler product dominates the harmonic sum.
concepts.c:harmonic-series: The divergent harmonic sum is pushed onto the primes.
